title: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The high proportion of flightless beetles on windswept islands such as Madeira is mainly due to natural selection favouring individuals that fly least and so avoid being blown out to sea, probably combined with disuse.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: these several considerations have made me believe that the wingless condition of so many Madeira beetles is mainly due to the action of natural selection, but combined probably with disuse.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.”. Scope: insects of oceanic islands, especially ground-living beetles

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The biogeographic association can be tested across islands and lineages using public records. Direct historical fitness evidence for Madeira is sparse, so the asserted main cause remains only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across island beetles, relate independent flight-loss transitions to wind exposure and model survival or dispersal loss at sea, with phylogenetic and habitat controls. More flightlessness and fitness advantage of reduced flight on windy islands support selection against wind loss.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Flightlessness and wing morphology are not comprehensively digitized.

Energetic economy, habitat stability and founder effects are rival explanations.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The wind-selection hypothesis makes a habitat prediction that can be scored if wing condition is compiled for Madeira and comparable islands. Occurrence databases supply localities, not the morphological variable, so the limiting step is collation. The exposed-versus-sheltered contrast has real discriminating power against a generic island effect and still leaves disuse as a joint cause, which the original wording already allows.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the proportion of flightless beetles between wind-exposed and sheltered habitats on Madeira and similar islands, and between those islands and mainland relatives. Higher flightlessness in exposed habitats would support selection by wind; equal rates in sheltered habitats and on calm islands would refute that specific agent. A residual role for disuse would remain if wing reduction also tracks lack of use within sheltered sites.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Madeira is well studied, but a global island-insect sample is patchy.

Disuse and wind selection predict overlapping reductions.

Wing state is not a field in occurrence databases and must be taken from faunas and specimens.
